Async operations (fetches, creates, lookups) can resolve out of order, or after the user has already moved on (signed out, cleared the chat, switched targets, started a newer request). Applying a stale result then silently overwrites newer, authoritative state — a classic race condition.

Whenever state is updated from an async callback, guard against staleness:
- Capture a generation/version number (or request id) before starting the async work.
- Bump that generation whenever an action invalidates in-flight work (reset, sign-out, clear, target switch, a newer request for the same key).
- Check the generation immediately before applying the result — not just at the start of the callback — since more invalidation can happen across multiple awaits.
- If the generation no longer matches, drop the result silently (and clean up any related loading/pending flags) instead of writing it into state.

```ts
const generationRef = useRef(0);

function reset() {
  generationRef.current++; // invalidate anything in flight
  setData(undefined);
}

async function load() {
  const generation = generationRef.current;
  const result = await fetchSomething();
  if (generation !== generationRef.current) return; // stale, drop it
  setData(result);
}
```

Where possible, prefer eliminating the race entirely rather than only patching it: let user actions be the single source of truth for state, and treat async lookups as read-only enrichment (e.g. resolving a display value from an id) rather than something that can overwrite what the user already chose. This removes an entire class of ordering bugs instead of requiring a generation check at every call site.

Every such guard should be covered by a regression test that starts a slow async operation, performs the invalidating action, then resolves the stale promise and asserts the stale result was dropped (and any side effects, like closing a spinner or detaching from a session, still ran correctly).
